A loss of top soil would be expected from such hydraulic action in the localized area of the ravine. Adverse effects on vegetation would occur in the immediate path of overflow waters. Localized adverse impacts would be expected for resident wildlife. Long-term adverse effects could result depending on the extent of surface damage. Short-term localized siltation and turbidity would be expected in Lake Jocassee similar to conditions previously described in Subsection 3.1.2.3 for high runoff into the lake.
3.2.2.3 Water Quality and Aquatic Fauna
Prior to filling and operation of the proposed Bad Creek Reservoir, the 4-foot diameter diversion pipe conveying water from the drainage into Howard Creek would be permanently closed with a concrete plug. Without any consideration of anticipated seepage or possible stream flow augmentation, this action would have the effect of reducing the measured flow in Howard Creek below its junction with Bad Creek by approximately 53 percent. Estimated flows from the Howard Creek drainage presented in Table 3-2 indicate that the runoff from the proposed project area is slightly greater than the flows derived from the Howard Creek drainage above Highway 171. A reduction of 25 percent or greater in stream flow would occur in Howard Creek as far downstream as Limber Pole Creek (Dysart et al., 1973). This represents about one-third of the length of the stream from Highway 413 to the junction of Howard Creek with Lake Jocassee. Above Highway 413, generally precipitous terrain and low tributary flows make Howard Creek less significant as trout water. Below Bad Creek junction during high or average spring stream flows, the overall effect of a 25 percent or greater reduction in the area of wetted stream bottom may not be significant. However, as natural flows decline with the advance of the summer or during years of unusually low flow, a 25 percent or greater flow reduction could produce adverse impacts on aquatic communities.
